title: Cerebral Vasculature Atlas
subtitle: Trace arterial territories, venous drainage, perforators and watershed zones
altText: Inferior and lateral brain views showing the Circle of Willis, anterior, middle and posterior cerebral arteries, perforators, watershed zones and venous drainage.
learningObjectives: Trace the internal carotid and vertebrobasilar circulations through the Circle of Willis.
Map ACA, MCA and PCA territories to characteristic neurobehavioural syndromes.
Recognise perforator, watershed and venous patterns that do not follow simple cortical territories.

sections.explainSimply: The brain receives blood through two paired arterial systems that join at its base and branch across the surface and deep structures.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Vascular territory often predicts the pattern and timing of cognitive, language, emotional and behavioural change, but collateral flow and individual anatomy create variability.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Anterior circulation derives primarily from internal carotid arteries; posterior circulation from vertebral arteries joining the basilar artery. The Circle of Willis permits collateral redistribution. Cortical branches, deep perforators and border zones produce distinct lesion patterns.
sections.thinkOfItLike: It is a city water network: major mains, ring connections, neighbourhood branches and tiny deep supply pipes each fail in different ways.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Sudden focal cognitive or behavioural change is a neurological emergency. Aphasia, neglect, amnesia or disinhibition may be the presenting sign of stroke.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Assuming stroke always presents with obvious weakness may miss posterior, right-hemisphere or strategically located infarcts.
sections.clinicalPearl: Territory maps are probabilistic: variant anatomy and collateral circulation can substantially alter the clinical picture.
sections.practicalExample: A dominant-hemisphere superior-division MCA infarct may produce nonfluent aphasia with relatively preserved comprehension.
sections.limitationsCautions: This atlas cannot determine an individual vascular lesion; acute symptoms require emergency stroke assessment and imaging.

anatomy.label: Circle of Willis
anatomy.function: Provides an arterial collateral ring at the brain base
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: Anatomical completeness varies; collateral competence cannot be assumed.

anatomy.label: Anterior cerebral artery
anatomy.function: Supplies medial frontal and parietal cortex
anatomy.connections: Corpus callosum and medial motor regions
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: Medial frontal injury may look psychiatric or motivational.

anatomy.label: Middle cerebral artery
anatomy.function: Supplies much of lateral cerebral cortex and deep lenticulostriate territories
anatomy.outputs: Superior, inferior and deep perforating divisions
anatomy.connections: Language, attention, motor and sensory networks
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: MCA syndromes vary markedly by hemisphere and division.

anatomy.label: Posterior cerebral artery
anatomy.function: Supplies occipital, inferomedial temporal and thalamic regions
anatomy.inputs: Basilar apex or fetal-origin internal carotid
anatomy.connections: Visual cortex, hippocampal and thalamic systems
anatomy.associatedDisorders: Visual field loss, alexia, memory disturbance
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: Posterior lesions can produce profound cognitive symptoms with little motor weakness.

anatomy.label: Watershed zones
anatomy.function: Border regions vulnerable to systemic hypoperfusion
anatomy.inputs: Distal ACA, MCA and PCA branches
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: Proximal limb weakness or higher cognitive deficits may follow hypotension.

anatomy.label: Deep perforators
anatomy.function: Supply internal capsule, basal ganglia, thalamus and brainstem
anatomy.inputs: MCA, ACA, PCA and basilar branches
anatomy.connections: Compact motor, sensory and arousal pathways
anatomy.associatedDisorders: Lacunar infarcts and strategic thalamic syndromes
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: Small lesions can cause dense deficits because deep pathways are tightly packed.
